The Election of 1912. Theodore Roosevelt, estranged from his successor William Howard Taft, launched a third-party Bull Moose campaign that captured more popular votes than Taft but gifted the presidency to Woodrow Wilson. The 1912 election split the Republican Party and ushered in an era of progressive reform, demonstrating the power of an insurgent progressive movement both within parties and outside them.

Roosevelt's platform—the most radical ever run by a major candidate—included women's suffrage, child labor laws, and expanded antitrust action. He ran as the Progressive Party candidate, winning twenty-seven percent of the popular vote and eighty-eight electoral votes. Taft, the incumbent Republican president, came third in popular votes with twenty-three percent but retained the Republican machinery and eight electoral votes. Wilson, the Democrat, won with just forty-two percent of the popular vote but four hundred thirty-five electoral votes, benefiting from the Republican split.

Eugene Debs, the Socialist candidate, received six percent of the popular vote—the Socialist Party's peak. Wilson's progressivism appealed to many potential Debs voters. The Bull Moose ticket split traditionally Republican voters, enabling Wilson to win nearly every state.

The GOP fractured, with progressives defecting to Roosevelt and moderates rallying to Taft; the party's center of gravity shifted rightward. The split proved permanent: the Republicans never reunited. By the nineteen twenties, the conservatives had reclaimed the party's leadership, and the progressives were permanently realigned as Democrats or independent voters.

Wilson took office with a mandate for reform, implementing tariff reduction, antitrust action, and Federal Reserve creation. The Federal Reserve would be created in 1913 by the Wilson administration this election enabled.
